objectives: Tell for-hire carriers, private fleets, owner-operators and brokers apart
Follow a load from booking to payment
Read the basic fields of a load posting
Explain what a dispatcher does and what they need from maintenance
body: Maintenance doesn't happen in a vacuum. Every repair decision lands on a load, a customer and a driver. This lesson gives you the vocabulary of the freight side of the business, so conversations with dispatch make sense from day one.

body.title: Types of carriers and freight companies

items.sub: Hauls other companies' freight for pay.
facts: USDOT number; interstate for-hire carriers also need FMCSA operating authority (currently identified by an MC number)
A truckload carrier moving retail freight for many shippers
items.watch: Uptime is revenue: every down unit is a load that isn't moving or a customer at risk.

items.sub: A company hauling its own goods.
facts: USDOT number for interstate commercial vehicles
A grocery chain delivering to its own stores
items.watch: Service to the company's own stores or plants drives priorities more than load revenue.

items.sub: A driver who owns (or leases) their truck.
facts: Often leased onto a carrier's authority; some run under their own authority
Set by the lease agreement — usually the owner-operator for their own truck
items.watch: Confirm who owns the unit before arranging or approving any repair.

items.sub: Arranges transportation between shippers and carriers — doesn't haul the freight.
facts: FMCSA broker authority and a $75,000 financial security (surety bond or trust)
Sends the carrier a rate confirmation for each load
items.watch: On brokered loads, the broker needs delay updates — through your dispatch team, following company procedure.

body.key: The same breakdown call can involve different decision-makers: your own fleet, an owner-operator, a chassis provider, or a broker waiting for an update. Ask who owns the unit and whose load it is.

body.title: The life of a load

items.d: Customer contract, broker or load board
Rate con: pickup, delivery, rate, rules

body.note: A breakdown can interrupt any step. The earlier it happens, the more options dispatch has — which is why fast, accurate ETRs matter.

body: Loads come from a carrier's own customer contracts, from freight brokers, or from load boards — online marketplaces where brokers and shippers post available loads and carriers post available trucks. The load details are then confirmed on a [[Rate confirmation|rate confirmation]].

body.title: Reading a load board posting (example)
rows: Posted all-in rate, or "call for rate"
Drop trailer at pickup; driver assist: no
body.note: Illustrative example — every load board and broker formats postings differently. Dispatch books loads; the coordinator needs to know the equipment and appointment details because they decide how urgent a repair is.

tiles.title: Plans loads
tiles.text: Matches loads to drivers, tractors and trailers — right equipment, right location, enough driver hours.

tiles.title: Tracks the trip
tiles.text: Watches location and ETA; handles check calls, delays and appointment changes.

tiles.title: Updates customers
tiles.text: Keeps shippers, receivers or brokers informed when something changes.

tiles.title: Recovers from problems
tiles.text: Reassigns loads, arranges power swaps or relays when equipment goes down.

callout.title: What dispatch needs from you
callout.text: Unit status, a realistic ETR with a confidence level, and early warning when it changes. Dispatch can only protect a load they know is at risk.

example.title: Whose truck is it?
example.text: A driver calls about a flat tire on a tractor that isn't in your fleet list. Before sending a vendor, the coordinator checks and learns it's an owner-operator leased onto the company. The lease says the owner-operator pays for their own repairs, so the coordinator connects the driver with a tire vendor, notes it on the load record, and tells dispatch the ETA — without approving charges on the company account.

exercise.prompt: Match each description to the type of company or person.

items.text: Arranges the move and sends the carrier a rate confirmation, but owns no trucks
A beverage company delivering its own products to its own warehouses
Driver who owns the tractor and is leased onto a larger carrier
items.why: Owns the equipment; works under a lease.

items.text: Hauls freight for many different shippers under its own operating authority
items.why: Paid to move other companies' freight.

o: A whiteboard in the terminal where dispatch tracks every truck
An online marketplace where loads and available trucks are posted
A government registry that lists every licensed carrier
The floor panel inside a dry van trailer
check.e: Brokers and shippers post loads; carriers post trucks and book loads.

check.q: A freight broker usually owns the trucks that haul its loads.
check.e: Brokers arrange transportation; carriers haul the freight.

check.q: Before arranging a repair on an unfamiliar tractor, what should you confirm first?
o: The driver's favorite shop in the area
Who owns the unit and who pays for repairs
The commodity code of the load on board
The tractor's model year and paint color
check.e: Ownership decides who authorizes and pays for the repair.

takeaways: Carriers haul; brokers arrange; private fleets haul their own goods; owner-operators own their trucks.
A load runs: booked → rate confirmed → dispatched → picked up → delivered → invoiced → paid.
Dispatch needs status, ETR and early warnings from maintenance.
tips: Learn your dispatch board's layout — it tells you which loads each repair affects.
Keep a list of owner-operator units and their repair arrangements.
mistakes: Approving a repair on a unit your company doesn't own.
Updating a broker directly when company procedure routes it through dispatch.

objectives: Apply HOS basics to repair timing
List the factors in a truck route and where maintenance fits
Use fuel data as an early maintenance signal
Know what IFTA is and who handles it
body: A repair that finishes "on time" can still fail the load if the driver is out of hours or the route to the delivery doesn't work. This lesson connects repair timing to the operational limits dispatch works with every day.

body.title: Hours of Service basics — property-carrying drivers (U.S.)

items.l: maximum driving after 10 consecutive hours off duty
on-duty window — no driving after the 14th hour, even with breaks
break after 8 cumulative hours of driving; any 30 straight minutes not driving counts, including shop time

body.note: Summary of FMCSA rules (49 CFR Part 395). Exceptions exist (short-haul, adverse driving conditions, sleeper-berth split and others). Dispatch and the safety department apply HOS — the coordinator uses it to judge whether a repair time still works for the load.

callout.title: Why the 14-hour window matters to you
callout.text: Waiting at a shop usually counts as on-duty time, and the 14-hour window keeps running. A 3-hour repair that starts late in a driver's day can mean the truck is fixed but the driver can't drive. Give dispatch ETRs early so they can plan a relay or a reset.

body.title: What goes into a truck route

items.d: Low clearances, weight limits, hazmat routes
PM due, known vendors on the lane

body: Truck routes are planned around restrictions cars never see: low bridges, weight-limited roads, hazmat restrictions and truck-prohibited routes. When you route a unit to a shop, the shop has to be reachable on a truck-legal route — and able to take the vehicle size.

Fuel is usually the largest variable cost in trucking. Fleets control it with fuel cards, preferred fuel networks and fuel surcharges billed to customers. For maintenance, fuel data is useful as an early-warning signal.

body.title: Fuel data as a maintenance signal
head: What the data shows
Possible maintenance causes
Coordinator action
rows: MPG drops on one unit, same lanes and loads
Underinflated tires, dragging brakes, aftertreatment or injector problems
Check recent faults; schedule an inspection
Driver comfort needs (HVAC, APU not working), or habit
Ask the driver; check APU/HVAC repair history
SCR/DEF system issue, or DEF purchases not captured
Fuel purchased with no miles driven
Unit in the shop, reefer fueling, or a data issue
Confirm with fuel records before assuming misuse
body.note: Patterns point to questions, not diagnoses. A technician confirms any mechanical cause.

body.title: Fuel tax and trip records: IFTA in brief
head: Question
Answer
rows: The International Fuel Tax Agreement among the 48 contiguous U.S. states and 10 Canadian provinces. Carriers report fuel and miles by jurisdiction on one quarterly return.
Generally, qualified motor vehicles used in interstate operation: two axles and over 26,000 lb, three or more axles, or a combination over 26,000 lb.
Miles driven to and from shops, and fuel bought during repairs, still belong in trip records. Accurate odometer readings on work orders help.
Usually accounting, fuel tax or safety/compliance staff — not the maintenance coordinator.
body.note: Overview only. Your base jurisdiction and your company's tax staff are the authority on IFTA reporting.

example.title: Fixed at 17:00 — delivered tomorrow
example.text: T-122 went into a shop at 12:30 with a starter failure; the driver had started duty at 06:00. The shop quoted three hours. The coordinator told dispatch right away: repair done around 15:30, leaving the driver about 4.5 hours in the 14-hour window, against a 5-hour run to delivery. Dispatch arranged a relay driver at the shop, and the load delivered on time. Had the ETR arrived at 17:00, the relay would have been too late to set up.

practical.title: Can the driver still make it?

exercise.prompt: Driver started duty at 05:00 and has driven 6 hours. The truck is at a shop; repair ETR is 14:30. Delivery is 4 hours of driving away. What should you tell dispatch?

options.text: Nothing — the truck will be fixed today.
options.why: Fixed isn't the same as able to deliver. The window matters.

options.text: At 14:30 the driver has 4.5 hours left in the 14-hour window (ends 19:00) and 5 hours of driving time. The shop wait already counts as the 30-minute break, so the 4-hour run fits with about 30 minutes to spare. Any delay at delivery uses up that margin, so flag the risk now.
options.why: Give dispatch the numbers early so they can decide on a relay or a new appointment. Since 2020, any 30 straight minutes off the wheel, including on-duty time at a shop, satisfies the break (49 CFR 395.3(a)(3)(ii)).

options.text: Tell the driver to log the shop wait as off duty so the clock stops.
options.why: Time waiting with the truck at a shop is usually on-duty time, and the 14-hour window keeps running either way. Never suggest how a driver should log. Dispatch and safety own HOS decisions.

check.q: A property-carrying driver starts duty at 06:00. When does the 14-hour driving window end?
o: It pauses during repairs
check.e: 06:00 + 14 hours = 20:00. The window keeps running during breaks and shop time.

check.q: A sudden MPG drop on one unit can be a maintenance signal.
check.e: Tire pressure, brakes and engine or aftertreatment issues can all raise fuel use.

check.q: Who usually prepares a carrier's IFTA return?
o: The maintenance coordinator
Accounting, fuel tax or compliance staff
The driver
The repair shop
check.e: The coordinator's part is accurate mileage on work orders and trip records.

takeaways: A repair ETR only helps if it fits the driver's remaining hours.
Shops must be reachable on truck-legal routes.
Fuel data can flag tire, brake and engine problems early.
IFTA is a quarterly fuel-tax report — handled by tax or compliance staff.
tips: Ask the driver's duty start time on every mid-day breakdown.
Keep fuel-economy outliers on your weekly review list.
mistakes: Giving a late ETR that leaves dispatch no time to arrange a relay.
Sending a unit to a shop it can't legally reach.

objectives: Explain what a trucking invoice is and why carriers issue one
Tell the shipper, broker, carrier, driver, receiver, factoring company and customer apart
Read the fields on a trucking invoice
body: An invoice is a bill: a document asking to be paid for work done. In trucking, the carrier — the company whose truck hauled the freight — sends an invoice after a load is delivered. No invoice, no payment. Even a perfect delivery earns nothing until it's invoiced correctly.

body.title: Who's who on a brokered load

items.d: Arranges the carrier; often pays it

head: Party
What they do
Role in the invoice
rows: The business sending the freight (e.g., a manufacturer)
Pays for transportation — directly to the carrier, or to a broker
A licensed intermediary that arranges transportation between shippers and carriers. Brokers don't haul freight themselves.
On brokered loads, the broker is usually who the carrier invoices
The trucking company that hauls the freight
Collects signed paperwork that proves the work was done
Signs the delivery paperwork — the proof of delivery
A finance company that buys carrier invoices
Pays the carrier early, then collects from the customer
The broker on a brokered load, or the shipper on a direct load

callout.title: Customer = whoever you bill
callout.text: On a brokered load the carrier's customer is the broker, not the shipper. On a direct load (no broker) the shipper is the customer.

body.title: Anatomy of a trucking invoice
lines: Crestline Freight Lines LLC · 100 Main St, Dallas TX · MC# 000000
Bill to: Northgate Freight Brokerage, Accounts Payable
Load # NFB-448213 · Dallas TX 06/12 → Atlanta GA 06/13 · 781 mi

notes.d: Legal name, address and authority number (MC or USDOT number) of the company being paid.
Exactly who is being billed — use their billing name and address.
A unique number, the invoice date and the payment terms (e.g., Net 30).
The customer's load/shipment number, pickup and delivery points and dates, and miles.
The agreed linehaul rate and any fuel surcharge.
Approved extras such as detention, layover, lumper and tolls — each with support.

tiles.title: Linehaul rate
tiles.text: The base price agreed for moving the load from pickup to delivery.

tiles.title: Fuel surcharge (FSC)
tiles.text: An amount that adjusts for diesel prices — a flat amount, per-mile, or included in an "all-in" rate, depending on the agreement.

tiles.title: Accessorial charges
tiles.text: Extra services beyond the basic move: detention, layover, lumper, tolls, extra stops and more.

tiles.title: Miles
tiles.text: Distance of the move — used to check rate per mile and some charges.

industry.name: Pro Transport USA
industry.text: Pro Transport, Inc. describes itself as a trucking and transportation provider founded in 1998, with its corporate office in Medley, Florida and terminals in Florida, Georgia and South Carolina. It serves local, regional and national customers with employees and owner-operators.
industry.relevance: This is an example of a carrier — the party that hauls freight and issues invoices for it. Each carrier sets its own billing process; this lesson teaches the common fundamentals.

example.title: A simple invoice, start to finish
example.text: Crestline hauled load NFB-448213 for Northgate Freight Brokerage. The rate confirmation said $1,900 linehaul plus $250 fuel surcharge. At delivery, the truck waited past the free time and the driver paid a lumper. Crestline's invoice to Northgate listed all four amounts with the supporting paperwork: $2,460.00 due under Net 30 terms.

exercise.source:
RATE CONFIRMATION — Northgate Freight Brokerage (fictional)
Carrier: Crestline Freight Lines LLC · MC# 000000 (fictional)
Load #: NFB-448213
Pickup: Dallas, TX · 06/12 08:00  |  Delivery: Atlanta, GA · 06/13 07:00
Equipment: 53' dry van · Miles: 781
Linehaul rate: $1,900.00   Fuel surcharge: $250.00 flat
Detention: $50/hr after 2 hours free · in/out times required on BOL
Lumper: reimbursed with receipt   Layover: $250/day   TONU: $150
Payment terms: Net 30 from receipt of invoice with signed POD

check.q: Who creates and sends the invoice for a brokered load?
o: The shipper
The broker
The carrier
The receiver
check.e: The carrier that hauled the freight invoices its customer — usually the broker on a brokered load.

check.q: A freight broker hauls freight with its own trucks.
check.e: Brokers arrange transportation; carriers haul it.

check.q: On a direct load with no broker, who is the carrier's customer?
o: The factoring company
The shipper
The driver
The receiver
check.e: Without a broker, the carrier bills the shipper directly.

takeaways: An invoice is the carrier's bill for a completed load.
Customer = whoever the carrier bills (broker or shipper).
Key fields: carrier & customer info, invoice #, date, terms, load #, route, rate, fuel, accessorials, total.
Every line must match what was agreed and what can be proven.
tips: Copy the customer's load number exactly from the rate confirmation.
Use one invoice-number sequence and never reuse a number.
mistakes: Billing the shipper when the broker is the customer.
Leaving off the load/reference number the customer uses to match payment.

objectives: Explain the purpose of the rate confirmation, BOL and POD
Match supporting documents to each charge
Spot missing paperwork before it delays payment
body: An invoice is a claim; documents are the evidence. Customers compare your invoice to the paperwork line by line. If a charge isn't supported, it's usually delayed or refused.

body.title: Documents and why they matter
head: Document
What it is
What it proves for payment
rows: The broker's written agreement with the carrier for this load: rate, stops, dates, accessorial terms
What the customer agreed to pay — every amount on the invoice should trace back to it
The shipping document issued at pickup describing the freight; a receipt for the goods and a contract for their transport
What was picked up, from whom, and where it was going
Delivery paperwork — often the BOL — signed by the receiver, with any shortages or damage noted
That the load was delivered. Most customers won't pay without it
A receiver's own receipt, when used
Receipt from a third-party unloading service
The lumper amount the carrier paid and wants reimbursed
In/out times at the facility — on the BOL, a signed time sheet, or electronic records
How long the truck waited beyond free time
Toll receipts, scale tickets, TONU confirmation, layover approval

body.title: The paper trail of one load

callout.title: Read the POD before you bill
callout.text: If the receiver wrote "2 cartons short" or "damaged" on the POD, the customer may reduce payment or open a claim. Know about exceptions before you submit — don't be surprised later.

body: Receivers often note OS&D — overage, shortage and damage — on the POD. A clean POD ("no exceptions") is the simplest to get paid on.

exercise.prompt: You're preparing the invoice for load NFB-448213 (linehaul, fuel, 2.5 h detention, $185 lumper). You have the rate confirmation and the signed POD. Which documents are still needed? (Select all that apply)

options.why: Supports the 2.5 billable hours — the rate con requires in/out times.
Fuel surcharge is set by the rate con, not by the driver's fuel purchases.

options.text: A second copy of the rate confirmation

example.title: The missing lumper receipt
example.text: A carrier billed $210 for a lumper but the driver lost the receipt. The broker paid the linehaul and held the lumper line. The carrier eventually got a copy from the receiving facility — two weeks later. Now its drivers photograph every receipt before leaving the dock.

practical.title: Match each charge to its support

exercise.prompt: Which document mainly supports each item?

items.why: The agreed rate comes from the rate con.
Proves how long the truck waited.

o: Proof of Delivery — signed delivery paperwork
Payment on Demand — invoice due on receipt
Point of Dispatch — where the load started
Price of Diesel — the fuel surcharge base
check.e: Proof of Delivery, usually the BOL signed by the receiver.

check.q: A charge on the invoice that isn't on the rate confirmation or otherwise approved will often be disputed.
check.e: Customers pay what they agreed to and what's supported.

takeaways: Rate con = what was agreed. BOL = what was shipped. POD = that it was delivered.
Every accessorial needs its own support.
Read the POD for exceptions before billing.
Missing paperwork is the #1 cause of slow payment.
tips: Ask drivers to photograph BOLs, PODs and receipts at the dock.
Build the invoice packet in the same order every time.
mistakes: Submitting an unsigned BOL as the POD.

objectives: Follow the invoicing workflow from load assignment to payment
Know what can go wrong at each step
Choose a submission method and run a pre-submission check

timeline.title: Load assigned
timeline.text: Dispatch books the load. Can go wrong: details agreed by phone never get confirmed in writing.

timeline.title: Rate confirmation received
timeline.text: Check rate, stops, dates and accessorial terms, then sign/return it per the broker's process. Can go wrong: wrong rate or missing detention terms nobody catches.

timeline.title: Load picked up
timeline.text: Driver checks the freight against the paperwork. Can go wrong: piece count differs from the BOL.

timeline.title: BOL collected
timeline.text: Driver keeps a clear copy. Can go wrong: illegible or lost BOL.

timeline.title: Delivery completed
timeline.text: In/out times recorded. Can go wrong: no times written — detention can't be proven.

timeline.title: POD signed
timeline.text: Receiver signs, prints name, notes exceptions. Can go wrong: no signature, or damage notes the office doesn't know about.

timeline.title: Supporting documents collected
timeline.text: Lumper and toll receipts, detention support. Can go wrong: receipts left in the truck for a week.

timeline.title: Invoice prepared
timeline.text: Every line traced to the rate con or approved extras. Can go wrong: typos in the load number or rate.

timeline.title: Documents attached
timeline.text: Rate con, POD and all supports in one packet. Can go wrong: one document missing = invoice on hold.

timeline.title: Invoice submitted
timeline.text: By the customer's required method. Can go wrong: sent to the wrong email or portal.

timeline.title: Broker/customer reviews
timeline.text: They match invoice to rate con and POD. Can go wrong: questions nobody answers.

timeline.title: Invoice approved
timeline.text: Scheduled for payment per terms. Can go wrong: short-paid with no explanation.

timeline.title: Payment processed
timeline.text: Payment received and applied. Can go wrong: payment can't be matched because the invoice number or load number was wrong.

body.title: Common submission methods
body.hint: A TMS (transportation management system) is software carriers use to manage loads, dispatch and billing. Which method you use is set by the customer or your factoring agreement.

body.title: Pre-submission checklist
rows: Matches the customer on the rate con
Exactly as on the rate con
Rate con, POD, receipts, time support

example.title: Portal vs email
example.text: A broker asked all carriers to use its online portal. One carrier kept emailing invoices to a general inbox — they sat unprocessed for three weeks. Once the carrier used the portal with the required fields, the next invoice was approved in four days.

exercise.prompt: Invoice CFL-1045 for NFB-448213: rate and load number match the rate con, total is $2,460, lumper receipt and detention times attached — but the POD photo is blurry and the receiver's signature can't be read. What do you do?

options.text: Submit now; they can ask if they need more
options.why: An unreadable POD is a common reason invoices are held or rejected.

options.text: Hold it, get a clear POD copy (from the driver or the receiver), then submit the complete packet
options.why: A complete, legible packet gets processed fastest.

options.text: Remove the detention and lumper to make it simpler
options.why: Those charges are valid and supported — don't give up earned money.

o: Truck Maintenance Schedule — the list of PM due dates
Transportation Management System — software for loads, dispatch and billing
Total Miles Summary — monthly miles by unit
Toll Management Service — billing for road tolls
check.e: TMS stands for transportation management system.

check.q: The broker requires invoices through its portal. You:
o: Email it anyway, since email is faster than a portal
Submit through the portal with required fields and attachments
Mail a paper copy with the signed documents
Wait until the broker asks for the invoice
check.e: Use the method the customer requires.

takeaways: Thirteen steps from load assignment to payment — each can fail.
Most problems start with missing or unclear paperwork.
Submit the way the customer requires.
Run the pre-submission checklist every time.
tips: Invoice the same day the POD arrives.
Keep a log of submission dates to track payment due dates.
mistakes: Waiting to batch invoices at month-end.
Submitting before all documents are in.

objectives: Identify common accessorial charges and their required support
Calculate payment due dates under Net terms
Explain freight factoring in neutral terms
body: An accessorial is a charge for a service beyond the basic pickup-to-delivery move. Whether and how much you can bill depends on the rate confirmation or a later written approval.

body.title: Common accessorials and their support
head: Charge
When it appears
Support usually needed
rows: Truck held at pickup or delivery beyond the free time (often 2 hours) in the agreement
In/out times on BOL or signed time sheet; timely notice to the broker if required
Driver held overnight or for a day because a load can't be loaded or delivered as scheduled
Load cancelled after the truck was dispatched or arrived
A third-party crew unloads (or loads) the freight; carrier pays and is reimbursed
Toll roads on the route, if the agreement allows billing them
An additional pickup or delivery location
Rate con or amendment listing the stop; signed paperwork at the stop
Approval and signed confirmation from the facility
Delivery attempt failed (e.g., receiver closed or refused) and the load is delivered again
Documentation of the failed attempt and approval
body.note: Terms vary by customer. If it isn't in the rate con, get written approval before (or when) the event happens.

body.title: When payment is due (invoice dated day 0)
body.note: "Net 30" means the full amount is due 30 days after the date the terms are measured from — often the invoice date or the date the complete invoice was received. Check the agreement.

body: Why terms matter: a carrier pays fuel, drivers and repairs every week. Waiting 30–60 days to be paid ties up cash. Late payments make it worse — so track due dates and follow up politely when an invoice passes its due date.

Factoring is when a carrier sells its invoices to a factoring company. The factoring company pays the carrier an advance quickly — often within a day or two — and then collects the full amount from the broker or shipper. In return it charges a fee, usually a percentage of the invoice. Terms such as advance rate, fees and "recourse" (whether the carrier must buy back an invoice the customer never pays) differ by agreement.

body.title: Example: factoring a $2,460 invoice (3% fee, 90% advance)
body.note: Later, after the customer pays the factoring company, the reserve ($246) minus the fee ($73.80) — $172.20 — is released. The carrier receives $2,386.20 in total. Numbers are illustrative; every agreement differs.

yes.title: Waiting for the customer
items: Paid on the customer's terms (e.g., Net 30)

no.title: Factoring
items: Pay a fee (a percentage of the invoice)
Factoring company handles collection; customer is told to pay the factor

example.title: The detention that almost wasn't
example.text: A driver waited 4 hours at a receiver. The rate con allowed detention after 2 free hours, but required notice to the broker when detention started. The dispatcher emailed the broker at the 2-hour mark with the arrival time — so the 2 billable hours were approved without argument.

exercise.source:
Invoice CFL-1045 dated 06/14 (terms measured from invoice date)
Customer A terms: Net 30
Customer B terms: Net 45
Factoring: 3% fee on a $2,460 invoice

o: Truck Ordered Not Used
Total Order Net Units
Transport Of Non-Urgent freight
Time Off Not Used
check.e: Truck Ordered Not Used — a charge when a load is cancelled after the truck was dispatched.

check.q: Arrived 06:40, departed 11:10, 2 hours free, $50/hour. Detention due?
check.e: 4.5 hours on site − 2 free hours = 2.5 billable × $50 = $125.

check.q: With factoring, the carrier usually receives payment sooner but pays a fee.

takeaways: Accessorials must be agreed (rate con or written approval) and supported.
Detention = time on site − free time, at the agreed rate.
Net 30/45/60 = days until payment is due.
Factoring trades a fee for faster cash.
tips: Notify the broker as soon as detention or layover begins, if the agreement requires it.
Keep a due-date list and follow up the day an invoice goes past due.
mistakes: Counting free time as billable detention.
Billing accessorials that were never approved.

objectives: Recognize the most common invoice errors
Correct and resubmit a rejected invoice
Build and check a complete trucking invoice

body.title: Common errors and how to fix them
head: Error
Example
How to correct & resubmit
rows: Correct to the rate con amount (or attach an approved rate change); resubmit with a note
Packet has rate con and BOL, no signed POD
Get the signed POD from the driver or receiver; resubmit the full packet
Invoice # skips or repeats your sequence
Void/correct per your accounting process; issue a proper unique number
Attach the receipt, or remove the line until it can be supported
Detention billed 4.5 h (free time not deducted)
Billed to the shipper instead of the broker
Re-issue to the correct bill-to name and address
Withdraw the duplicate; confirm only one is open
Correct the reference exactly as on the rate con
Obtain a signed POD or the receiver's delivery confirmation
body.note: When resubmitting, say what changed ("Corrected load # per rate con") and follow the customer's process for revised invoices.

body.title: Why invoices were held (example carrier, one quarter)
body.note: Illustrative numbers. Paperwork problems — not disputes — cause most payment delays.

msg.title: Draft invoice — CFL-1046
msg.text:
Bill to: Northgate Freight Brokerage
Load #: NFB-448231

exercise.prompt: Compare the draft to the rate confirmation and delivery details (load NFB-448213, $1,900 linehaul, $250 FSC, 2 h free time, arrived 06:40 / departed 11:10). Which errors are present? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Load number is transposed (…231 instead of …213)
options.why: The reference must match the rate con exactly.

body: Now build the correct invoice for load NFB-448213 from the rate confirmation and delivery details. The preview updates as you type.

example.title: Rejected, fixed, paid
example.text: A broker rejected an invoice with the note "POD missing receiver signature." The carrier asked the receiving facility for its signed copy, attached it, added "Resubmitted with signed POD" to the note field, and resubmitted through the portal the same day. It was approved on the next review cycle.

exercise.prompt: Match each rejection message to its reason.

check.q: An invoice is rejected for a mismatched load number. Best fix?
o: Resubmit it unchanged; the broker will match it by amount
Correct the load number exactly as on the rate con and resubmit with a note
Create a new load with the broker's number and invoice that
Call the shipper and ask them to approve the invoice
check.e: Fix the reference and explain the correction.

check.q: Sending the same invoice twice "just in case" helps you get paid faster.

takeaways: Most rejections are paperwork and reference errors.
Correct the specific problem and say what changed.
Build every invoice from the rate con and delivery documents.
Check before you submit — it's faster than fixing after.
tips: Keep a rejection log — patterns show what to fix in your process.
Double-check digits in load numbers; transpositions are common.
mistakes: Resubmitting without fixing the root problem.
Issuing a new invoice number for a correction without voiding the old one.
